subject: 정당한 전쟁의 조건
title: What must hold before fighting is permitted
content: A tradition running back many centuries holds that war can be justified, but only under conditions that are demanding and cumulative. Each condition must be satisfied, and satisfying most of them is not enough, which is what distinguishes this moral framework from a general licence to fight for good causes. The first condition concerns the cause. Only defence against an attack, or the prevention of a grave wrong, has generally been accepted, and the list of admissible causes has narrowed considerably across the centuries as claims about honour and religion were removed from it. The second concerns authority, since a decision of this magnitude must be taken by those answerable for it rather than by anybody who judges the cause good. Three further conditions concern proportion and prospect. The harm expected must not exceed the wrong prevented, there must be a reasonable chance of success, and every alternative short of force must have been genuinely attempted rather than merely mentioned. The last is where most historical justifications actually fail, since negotiations are frequently abandoned when they become inconvenient rather than when they become hopeless. A final condition concerns intention. A state fighting for an admissible cause while actually pursuing something else has not satisfied the framework, and the tradition insists on this even though intention is unverifiable. The point is that the moral assessment concerns what is being sought rather than what is being claimed. Critics argue that the framework has served mainly to supply language for whatever states intended to do, and the historical record gives that charge real force. The reply is that a framework which can be abused is still better than none, since it supplies terms in which an unjust war can be criticised, and every serious criticism of a modern war has in fact been conducted in exactly these terms.

subject: 도덕적 의견 불일치가 뜻하는 것
title: What persistent moral disagreement shows
content: People disagree about moral questions, and the disagreement persists across centuries and cultures without converging in the way that disagreement about the natural world tends to. Some philosophers treat this as evidence that there is nothing to be right about, and the argument deserves examination rather than dismissal. The strongest version runs as follows. Where inquiry is tracking a truth, informed and careful investigators tend toward agreement over time, and the history of the sciences shows exactly that pattern. Moral inquiry shows nothing comparable, so the best explanation is that no truth is being tracked and moral claims express something else. Several replies have force. The first observes that agreement is greater than the argument allows, since disputes cluster around a small number of contested questions while an enormous body of shared judgment goes unremarked precisely because nobody contests it. Nobody argues about whether gratuitous cruelty is wrong. The second reply notes that many apparent moral disagreements rest on factual disagreements. Two people may share a principle about harm while differing about what a practice actually does, and that difference is empirical rather than moral. Historical cases support this, since several moral changes followed the correction of factual beliefs rather than any shift in values. A third reply concerns interest. Moral questions differ from scientific ones in that the answers bear directly on how people may live and what they must give up, so we should expect resistance to correct answers that scientific questions do not provoke. Persistent disagreement about taxation is not evidence that no answer exists. What survives is a genuine puzzle rather than a proof. The argument establishes that moral knowledge, if there is any, is harder to secure and slower to spread than the natural kind, which almost nobody would deny.

subject: 기억은 얼마나 믿을 만한가
title: Trusting what you remember
content: Nearly all that a person believes about their own past rests on memory, and memory gives no separate check on itself. When I recall an event, I do not hold the memory up against the event; I simply have the memory, and its vividness is what wins me over. Whether that is enough ground for belief is a real question about knowledge. Yet the evidence here is not encouraging. Remembering rebuilds rather than replays, so each such act puts the scene together again from its pieces, filling the gaps with what was likely. So details drift, and firm detailed memories of events that never took place can be planted under quite ordinary conditions. Being sure and being right go together only weakly, and therefore this removes the one sign that people actually use. Yet the doubting view goes too far. If memory failed us in general, ordinary life would be impossible, and the very studies that show its faults were run by people relying on notes and on their own memory of the method. These failures gather in known settings: long gaps, high feeling, repeated questioning, and events much like many others. Although fine detail drifts, memory for the broad shape of a life is far more solid. What follows from this is a discipline rather than a doubt. Where a memory concerns something checkable, checking is worth the trouble, and where it concerns a disputed matter, the confidence attached to it should not be treated as evidence of its accuracy. This bears heavily on testimony in legal settings, where a witness's certainty is precisely what persuades a jury and precisely what fails to predict correctness. The deeper moral point is about how we treat other people's accounts. Somebody whose recollection differs from ours has not necessarily lied, and treating disagreement about the past as evidence of dishonesty misunderstands what remembering actually is.

subject: 동료의 반대에 부딪혔을 때
title: When somebody just as able disagrees
content: Suppose you have thought carefully about a question and therefore reached a conclusion. Then you learn that somebody equally informed and equally careful has reached the opposite view. What should happen to your confidence is a question that has generated considerable philosophical argument, and the available answers are all uncomfortable. One position holds that you should therefore move substantially toward the other view. If you have no reason to think yourself better placed, then treating your own judgment as decisive amounts to giving yourself an authority you cannot justify, and the honest response splits the difference. Although this has real force, it carries an awkward consequence, because it appears to make sustained conviction irrational for anybody aware that experts disagree. The opposing position holds that you may retain your view. You have examined the arguments and found them convincing, and since that examination is evidence you hold and the other party does not, treating their disagreement as decisive discards what you actually know. The difficulty here is that the other party can reason identically, and both cannot be right. A middle position attends to what the disagreement reveals. Where you can identify a specific reason the other party might have gone wrong, your confidence may reasonably survive; where you cannot, the disagreement is evidence that one of you has erred and you have no ground for assuming it was them. The practical stakes are considerable. Somebody who never adjusts for disagreement will hold false views permanently, whereas somebody who always adjusts will hold no views at all in any contested domain. What the argument finally recommends is attending to whether the other party is genuinely as informed, since most actual disagreements involve an asymmetry that one side has not noticed, and finding it is more useful than any general rule.

subject: 향의 문화와 기억
title: Burning resin inside a sacred room
content: Ritual use of scent appears in temples, churches, and shrines across a remarkable range of unconnected traditions. The materials differ — resins from one region, sandalwood from another, herbs where nothing is imported — and yet the practice of filling a religious space with smoke recurs so widely that it deserves explanation as a cultural technique rather than as a local custom. Its effect is architectural. Smoke makes a shaft of light visible, so a beam entering a high window becomes a solid object that a congregation can see, and the volume of the room is revealed in a way that empty air does not permit. Buildings designed for such use place their openings accordingly, and the interaction between the light, the smoke, and the height was clearly intended by those who built them. The material was frequently expensive. Certain resins travelled thousands of kilometres by caravan and ship, and burning them consumed in an hour what represented substantial value, so the practice itself was a form of offering. Communities that could not obtain the traditional material substituted local plants, and the substitutions are recorded in the archaeology of the sites. Scent also marks a boundary. Crossing from ordinary air into a space with a distinct smell announces that one has entered somewhere different, and the association forms quickly and persists, which is why participants raised in a tradition report an immediate response decades after leaving it. The effect is learned rather than intrinsic. What the practice illustrates is an aesthetic dimension that architectural history has largely ignored. Buildings are studied through their plans and elevations, and yet the experience of being inside one was shaped by an element that leaves no trace in any drawing and survives only in accounts, in the vessels recovered, and in the traditions that continue.

subject: 단순성은 왜 미덕인가
title: Why we prefer the simpler explanation
content: When two accounts explain the same evidence, we generally prefer the simpler one. The preference is ancient, it operates throughout the sciences, and it seems obviously correct until somebody asks why simplicity should indicate truth. Nothing guarantees that the world is simple, and stating the justification turns out to be surprisingly hard. One answer is pragmatic. Simpler theories are easier to use, easier to test, and easier to teach, so preferring them is a decision about convenience rather than a claim about truth. This is honest and it does not explain why simplicity so frequently succeeds, since a preference based purely on convenience should not predict correctness as reliably as it appears to. A second answer treats simplicity as bound up with evidence. A complicated account with many adjustable parts can accommodate any observation, so it forbids nothing and the evidence never tests it. A simple account makes sharper predictions and therefore risks more, and when it survives, that survival means more. On this reading simplicity is a proxy for testability rather than a virtue in itself, which is a considerably more defensible position. A third answer notes that added complexity requires justification. Every extra element in a theory is an additional claim about the world, and each claim can be wrong, so a theory with more parts has more ways of being false. This is close to a probabilistic argument and it has been made precisely in several formal frameworks. What none of these answers supplies is a guarantee. The world contains genuinely complicated arrangements, and preferring simplicity has occasionally delayed the acceptance of a correct but messy account. The principle is therefore a defeasible guide about which theory deserves to be tested first rather than a truth about how things are.

subject: 가구 양식이 말하는 생활 방식
title: What chairs and tables record about a household
content: Furniture survives in quantity from the past few centuries, and it carries information about daily life that written sources rarely supply. A chair records how somebody sat, what they wore, how long they expected to remain, and who was permitted to sit at all, and reading these objects has become a recognised branch of cultural history. Seating is the most informative category. A society in which most people sat on the floor or on benches developed different domestic architecture from one in which individual chairs were standard, and the transition can be dated in several regions. Where a single chair with arms stood among stools, the arrangement recorded authority within the household, and the vocabulary of the chair still preserves that association in several languages. The construction reveals economic conditions. Joined furniture requires a skilled craftsman and seasoned timber; boarded furniture can be made by anybody with planks and nails, and the ratio between them in surviving inventories indicates what a region could afford. Veneer and inlay appear where thin sheets of costly wood could be applied over cheap carcass timber, which is a technique that responds to price rather than to taste. Storage furniture tracks what households owned. Chests give way to chests of drawers as the quantity of clothing increases, and specialised cabinets appear as new categories of possession arrive: china, books, papers, instruments. Each new form marks something that had become common enough to need a place. What makes such objects unusually good evidence is that they were made to be used rather than to be admired. Nobody arranged a kitchen table to impress posterity, so the traces of wear, repair, and alteration record actual practice, and a piece that was cut down, extended, or rebuilt tells more about the household than any inventory could.

subject: 무대 의상이 시대를 지시하는 방식
title: Telling an audience when a play is set
content: A production must inform the audience of its period within seconds, and costume does most of that work. What is remarkable is how few elements are actually required, since audiences read a period from a small number of signals and supply the rest themselves. Silhouette carries the information almost entirely. A particular shoulder line, waist position, or skirt volume identifies a decade to viewers who could not name a single garment, and designers exploit this by getting the outline right and treating the detail loosely. A production may combine fabrics and finishes from several eras without the audience noticing, provided the shape is consistent. The choice of period is itself an argument. Staging an old play in modern dress asserts that its concerns are current, and doing so removes the historical distance that would otherwise let an audience treat the events as belonging to somebody else. Setting a modern play in an earlier era does the opposite, creating a distance that permits difficult material to be examined. Neither choice is neutral, and directors state their reasons in exactly these terms. Mixed period design has become common and is harder to read. Placing one character in contemporary clothing among others in historical dress marks them as outside the world of the play, and productions use this to indicate a narrator, a ghost, or somebody whose perspective the audience shares. The device works only because the audience has learned the convention. What underlies all of this is that period signals are cultural rather than factual. Audiences recognise a decade by the version of it that films and photographs have taught them, which is frequently a stylised composite rather than what people actually wore, and a designer who dressed a production with strict accuracy would frequently fail to communicate the period at all.

subject: 통계적 증거만으로 판결할 수 있는가
title: Convicting somebody on a probability
content: Suppose a hundred people were present, and it is established that ninety nine of them participated in a wrong. A given individual is therefore overwhelmingly likely to be liable, and yet almost every legal system refuses to decide against them on that evidence alone. Explaining the refusal is a genuine problem, since the probability exceeds what other kinds of evidence typically deliver. The puzzle sharpens by comparison. A single witness identifying somebody is accepted despite well documented rates of error that may be worse than one in a hundred. So the objection cannot be about the numbers, and something other than probability must be doing the work in our judgments. One proposed answer concerns individual evidence. Statistical evidence bears on somebody only through their membership in a group, whereas a witness account bears on them specifically, and a verdict should rest on facts about the person rather than on facts about a class they belong to. This captures the intuition, although stating it precisely has proved difficult. A second answer concerns what would have happened otherwise. Testimony would have been different had the person been innocent, whereas the statistic would have been exactly the same, so the statistical evidence fails to track the individual's actual conduct in the way that other evidence does. A third answer is practical. A system convicting on base rates alone would give people no way to avoid liability through their own behaviour, since nothing they did would change the number. That consequence undermines the point of holding anybody responsible. What the puzzle finally illuminates is that legal proof was never simply about probability. The demand is for evidence that connects to this person, and treating the question as arithmetic misses what a verdict is supposed to establish.

subject: 민속춤의 대형과 공동체 구조
title: What a dance formation says about a village
content: Traditional dances organise people in space, and the arrangements are remarkably varied: closed circles, open chains, facing lines, and couples in a set. These formations are not arbitrary decoration, since each permits different relationships among the dancers, and comparing them across cultures reveals patterns worth attention. A closed circle admits everybody and ranks nobody. Each dancer holds the hands of two neighbours, all face inward, and no position is superior, so the form expresses a community of equals and is frequently used at occasions concerning the whole village. Adding a leader who directs the figures introduces a single distinguished role while keeping the rest undifferentiated. An open chain behaves differently. The line has a head and a tail, the leader is visible and may improvise while the others follow, and joining at the end is possible at any moment. Such forms accommodate arrivals and departures, which suits an occasion that continues for hours and that people attend intermittently. Facing lines create a different relation again, since two groups confront one another and may represent men and women, two families, or two parts of a settlement. Dances of this shape frequently accompany occasions concerned with alliance, and the figures involve the two lines exchanging places, which is a fairly direct enactment of what the occasion concerns. Couple dances are historically recent in most traditions and were resisted where they appeared, precisely because pairing two people privately within a public gathering altered what the occasion meant. The objections recorded at the time were about the social form rather than about the movement. What all of this suggests is that a dance tradition encodes a community's understanding of itself, and that changes in the formations track changes in how people expect to relate to one another.

subject: 가면극의 즉흥과 대본
title: Playing without a script that anybody wrote
content: Several masked traditions were played for centuries with no written text. Players held an order of scenes, a set of figures, and a stock of routines, and the words were made fresh at each showing. Seeing how such a tradition keeps itself alive, and what happens when somebody finally writes it down, lights up the whole tie between text and playing. This material is held in units. A player knows a great many set pieces — a lament, a boast, a quarrel, a comic mix up — each of which can be drawn out or cut short by how the crowd is taking it. A scene is built by picking and joining these units, and therefore the show is put together as it goes from parts made ready long before. This is just the method that oral epic singers use. Because none of it is written, this craft passes by apprenticeship. A young player learns by taking small parts beside somebody who holds the tradition, taking in timing, the stock routines, and the bounds within which invention is allowed. Nothing is taught by telling, and those who do it often cannot state the rules they follow, which leaves such traditions very open to being broken. One lost generation wipes out what centuries had built up. Writing these plays down changes them. A published text becomes authoritative, so later performers treat departure from it as error, and although improvisation had sustained the form for centuries, it now counts as a violation of the script. Several such traditions were recorded by folklorists precisely when they were declining, and that recording froze them in whatever state they happened to be in. What is preserved afterwards is therefore a photograph rather than a practice, and companies reviving this work face a real choice between performing its text faithfully and recovering the method that produced it.

subject: 기하 문양의 전파와 변형
title: Patterns that travelled without their meaning
content: Certain geometric designs appear across enormous distances and among peoples with no plausible contact: interlocking spirals, meanders, stepped frets, and eight pointed stars. Explaining these recurrences has occupied art historians for a long time, and the answers turn out to be several rather than one. Some recurrence is independent invention. A limited number of patterns can be produced by weaving, plaiting, or basketry, since the crossing of warp and weft generates steps and diagonals naturally, and any culture working in those materials will arrive at similar results. Designs that originate in a technique are therefore expected to appear wherever the technique does, and no diffusion need be involved. Other recurrences do record contact. Motifs travelled on portable objects — textiles, ceramics, metalwork — and were copied by craftsmen who admired them, so a design can be traced along trade routes with reasonable confidence when its variants form a geographic sequence. Islamic geometric ornament spread this way across three continents, and its arrival in each region is datable. What almost never travels is the meaning. A pattern that carried a specific significance in one culture is adopted elsewhere for its appearance, and the borrowing tradition attaches its own meaning or none at all. Consequently identical designs may be sacred in one place and merely decorative in another, and inferring shared belief from shared ornament is among the standard errors in the field. Nineteenth century scholarship made exactly that inference repeatedly, constructing migrations and ancient connections from motif similarities alone. The correction came from attending to technique and to sequence rather than to resemblance. Two patterns that look alike may share an origin, a material, or nothing whatever, and distinguishing these possibilities requires evidence beyond the design itself.

subject: 의식은 왜 설명하기 어려운가
title: The problem that will not dissolve
content: Scientific accounts of the mind have advanced enormously. We can say which structures are involved in vision, what happens when attention shifts, and how anaesthesia works, and yet one question appears untouched by all of it: why any of this activity should be accompanied by experience at all. The difficulty has a specific shape. Explaining a function is one thing, and neuroscience does it well. Explaining why performing that function feels like something is a different demand, since one can describe the entire causal story of colour vision without saying anything about why the resulting state has a quality for the person in it. A complete functional account seems logically compatible with there being no experience whatever, and that compatibility is what makes the problem hard rather than merely unsolved. Several responses are available. One denies the gap, holding that our sense that something remains unexplained reflects a confusion in how we think about ourselves rather than a genuine further fact. Once every function is accounted for, nothing is left over, and the impression of a residue is an artefact of the concepts we use. This position is coherent and many find it impossible to believe. Another response accepts the gap and treats experience as fundamental, appearing wherever certain arrangements occur rather than being produced by them. This solves the explanatory problem by declining to explain, which critics regard as a retreat rather than an answer. A third holds that our concepts are simply inadequate and that a future framework will dissolve the question, although nobody can say what such a framework would look like. What makes the dispute unusual is that everybody agrees on the empirical facts. The disagreement concerns what would count as an explanation, which is a philosophical question rather than a scientific one, and no experiment settles it.

subject: 정물화가 사물에 부여한 의미
title: When objects stopped standing for anything
content: Still life painting began as a form loaded with meaning, in which each object carried an association that contemporaries read fluently. Over several centuries the tradition moved away from that, and by the late nineteenth century painters were arranging fruit and cloth on a table with no symbolic intention whatever. Understanding that shift illuminates a larger change in what painting was for. The earlier practice required a shared vocabulary. A viewer had to know what a particular flower or a cut lemon indicated, and the pleasure of such pictures included the pleasure of reading them. Once that vocabulary faded, the paintings did not become meaningless; they became difficult, which is why so much scholarship is devoted to recovering associations that the first audiences absorbed without instruction. The later practice made the objects a pretext. A painter working with apples and a jug was interested in how form, colour, and the relations between shapes could be organised, and the subject was chosen precisely because nobody would be distracted by it. This is why the genre became central to the development of modern painting, since it permitted formal experiment without the narrative demands that figures bring. The objects themselves became more assertive as their symbolism disappeared. Painters emphasised weight, surface, and the way one thing sits against another, and critics began writing about the presence of the depicted things rather than their significance. A jug in such a picture is not standing for anything and is not merely a shape either. What the whole trajectory demonstrates is that a genre can survive the loss of its original purpose by acquiring another. Nothing about arranging objects on a table required either symbolic reading or formal experiment, and the tradition supported both across four centuries without either being obvious from the subject matter.

subject: 오페라의 번역과 상연
title: Singing a work in a language it was not written for
content: An opera composed in one language may be staged in another, and companies have argued about this for two centuries. The dispute is not merely practical, since each option changes the work in ways that neither side denies. Singing it translated makes the words plain without a screen, and this restores something the first audience had. Comedy in particular depends on timing, and a joke that arrives three seconds later on a caption above the stage is not a joke. Traditions of translated performance developed strong conventions, and several countries maintained them as the normal practice for a century or more. Yet its cost is considerable. A composer sets particular syllables to particular notes, and vowel sounds determine what a singer can do at a given pitch, so a translation that preserves the meaning frequently forces vowels that are difficult or ugly where the original was comfortable. Those working in this art face tighter limits than any other kind of translation, since they must match sense, stress, rhyme, and singability at once. The arrival of surtitles changed this argument. Audiences could follow the text while hearing the original sound, and most major houses moved to performing in the original language within a decade of the technology arriving. Critics of that shift point out that reading during a performance splits attention, and that audiences now watch a screen rather than the stage during its most important passages. What this debate finally concerns is which loss to accept. Performing in translation damages the relation between the words and the music; performing in the original damages the relation between the audience and the drama. No arrangement avoids both, and companies that have tried alternating between them report that the audiences for each are largely different people.

subject: 민화의 익명성과 유통
title: Pictures sold in markets and signed by nobody
content: Popular painting in most traditions circulated as a commodity. Pictures were produced in workshops, sold at markets or by peddlers, bought for a specific occasion, and replaced when they wore out, and this pattern of production and use explains more about the objects than any account of their style. Speed was essential. A painter supplying a market worked at a price the buyer could afford, so a picture had to be finished in hours rather than weeks, and the techniques developed accordingly: limited palettes, confident outlines, stencils for repeated elements, and multiple copies made side by side. What looks like naive handling frequently reflects a production rate rather than a lack of training. The subjects repeated because buyers wanted particular things. A picture bought for a wedding, for a new house, or for a shop had a function, and departing from the expected image would have made it useless to the customer. Consequently workshops competed on handling and price rather than on invention, and the surviving variety within a single subject shows exactly where invention was permitted. Nobody signed. Attribution was irrelevant to a buyer choosing among similar pictures at a stall, and the workshop rather than the individual was the unit of production, so almost no names survive from traditions that produced hundreds of thousands of paintings. This is the principal reason such work entered art history late, since the discipline was organised around named artists. Survival was accidental and heavily biased. Pictures were pasted to walls, exposed to smoke, and discarded when replaced, so what remains is what happened to be stored or collected, and collectors chose according to their own taste. The corpus available for study is therefore a filtered sample of a tradition whose ordinary output has largely disappeared.

subject: 개인 동일성은 무엇이 유지하는가
title: What makes you the same person as before
content: A person changes continuously. The matter composing their body is replaced, their beliefs shift, their memories fade, and their character develops, and yet we treat them as one person across a whole life. What that continuity consists of is a question with practical consequences for responsibility, for promising, and for what a person may be held to. One answer appeals to the body. Somebody is the same person as before if they are the same living organism, which has the advantage of being objective and continuous. It has the awkward consequence that a person whose psychological life had been entirely replaced would still be the same person, and most intuitions resist that. A second answer appeals to psychological connections. Memory, intention, and character link each stage of a life to the next, and identity consists in those chains rather than in any underlying thing. This fits our judgments about many imagined cases and creates a difficulty of its own, since such connections come in degrees, and identity does not appear to. Either somebody is you or they are not. A third position accepts the difficulty and concludes that identity matters less than we assume. What we actually care about is the psychological continuity, and where that is present in degrees, our concern should be proportional. On this reading the question of whether a future person will be you is not always answerable, and the practical questions can be settled without answering it. The consequences reach into ordinary life. How much a person owes for something done decades earlier, whether an advance directive binds somebody whose mind has changed, and what obligations run to one's own future all depend on the answer, and courts and families settle these questions daily using assumptions that no philosophical account has fully vindicated.

subject: 전통 공예의 전수 방식
title: Knowledge that passes through the hands
content: A craft tradition survives because somebody teaches it, and the teaching rarely resembles instruction. An apprentice watches, assists, and is given progressively harder work, and much of what they acquire was never stated by anybody, because the person teaching cannot state it either. Understanding this explains why such traditions are so difficult to revive once broken. The knowledge is largely in judgment. A potter knows when clay is ready by how it resists the hand, a smith reads temperature by colour, and a weaver adjusts tension by feel, and none of these judgments can be conveyed by a number. They are learned by doing the thing beside somebody who corrects the attempt, and the correction is frequently physical rather than verbal. Sequence matters as much as content. Traditions typically assign years of preparatory work — grinding pigment, preparing materials, cleaning tools — before the apprentice touches the principal operation, and outsiders frequently read this as exploitation. Practitioners describe it differently, arguing that the preparatory work builds exactly the perceptual discrimination the later work requires, and that somebody who skips it cannot see what they are doing wrong. Documentation captures very little. Films, manuals, and interviews record the visible steps while missing the judgments, and traditions reconstructed from such records typically produce objects that specialists identify immediately as wrong without being able to say why. Several national programmes designating living practitioners as holders of a tradition exist precisely because the alternative preservation methods fail. The vulnerability is therefore structural. A craft can be lost within one generation if the economic conditions that supported apprenticeship disappear, and no archive prevents it, since what would need to be archived is a capacity rather than a description.

subject: 색유리가 만든 종교 공간
title: Walls of coloured light
content: Stained glass transformed what a building could do. A wall of coloured glass admits light while altering it, so the interior is filled with a shifting illumination that changes with the weather and the hour, and the medieval architecture of northern Europe was reorganised around making such walls possible. The engineering came first. Filling a wall with glass requires that the wall stop carrying weight, so the load had to be transferred to piers and then outward to external supports, and the whole system of pointed arches, ribbed vaults, and flying buttresses was developed to permit openings that earlier construction could not have survived. The aesthetic ambition drove the structural innovation rather than following it. The colour was made in the glass rather than applied to it. Metal oxides added to the molten batch produce blue, red, and green throughout the material, and the medieval blues in particular have never been exactly reproduced, since the recipes were not written down and the raw materials differed. Details were painted on in a dark pigment and fired, and the lead framework that holds the pieces is part of the design rather than an intrusion, carrying the strongest lines of the composition. The programmes were didactic and are frequently described as instruction for those who could not read. This is partly true and considerably overstated, since the windows are high, the scenes are small, and the sequence is difficult to follow from the floor. A more defensible account emphasises the light itself, which contemporaries described in theological terms as a manifestation rather than as illustration. What survives has been heavily restored, and much was destroyed deliberately in periods of religious conflict. Reading a window now requires distinguishing medieval glass from later replacement, which specialists do by the colour and the surface corrosion rather than by the imagery.

subject: 자기 지식의 특권
title: Knowing your own mind
content: A person seems to know their own thoughts in a way that nobody else can match. I do not observe my own belief or infer it from my behaviour; I simply know what I think, and if somebody contradicts me about it we ordinarily assume I am right. Explaining this apparent privilege has proved considerably harder than the phenomenon suggests. One account treats it as inner observation. Just as I know the room by looking, I know my mind by attending to it, and my superior access reflects my position. This picture is intuitive and faces serious objections, since it posits an inner sense whose workings nobody can describe, and it predicts errors of observation that ordinary self knowledge does not seem to make. A second account denies that observation is involved. Knowing that I believe something is not a matter of detecting a state but of being prepared to assert it, so the question of what I believe is answered by considering the matter itself rather than by examining myself. This explains why introspection about belief feels like thinking about the world rather than looking inward. The evidence complicates any simple privilege. People are demonstrably wrong about why they did things, constructing explanations after the fact that experiment shows to be false, and they misjudge their own attitudes in ways that others detect more accurately. So the privilege, whatever it is, does not extend to motives or to character. What survives is a narrower claim. A person has a special authority about what they currently think and intend, and much less about why, and treating the two as one has caused a good deal of confusion in moral argument. Somebody sincerely reporting their reason may be sincerely wrong, and recognising this changes how their testimony about themselves should be weighed.

subject: 거울이 회화에 들어온 순간
title: When painters started putting mirrors in pictures
content: Mirrors appear in European painting from the fifteenth century onward, and their arrival coincides with the availability of glass mirrors that produced a clear image. Painters began including them almost immediately, and what they did with them goes well beyond depicting a household object. A mirror lets a painting show what lies outside its own frame. A convex glass on the back wall of a room can reflect the space in front of the picture, including figures the viewer cannot otherwise see, so the painted world extends into the position the viewer occupies. Several celebrated works use exactly this device, and the effect is that the audience discovers themselves implicated in the scene. It also permits two views of one thing. A figure seen from behind may be reflected from the front, which demonstrates the painter's command of form while asserting that painting can accomplish what sculpture claims as its advantage. Renaissance arguments about the relative merits of the two arts were conducted partly through such demonstrations, and the mirror was the instrument. The device carried meaning as well. Mirrors were associated with vanity, with self knowledge, and with truthfulness, so including one made a claim about the picture. A painter depicting their own reflection asserted a presence within the work, and self portraits made with the aid of a mirror carry a characteristic direct gaze that results from the method. Later traditions kept the device and changed its use. Nineteenth century painters placed mirrors behind bars and in dressing rooms to show the same figure twice, one presented and one observed, and the resulting ambiguity about which view is truer became the subject of the picture. What began as a technical opportunity had become a way of asking what a painted image shows.

subject: 동화의 잔혹성과 그 편집사
title: How the cruelty was edited out of fairy tales
content: The stories collected by folklorists in the nineteenth century were considerably harsher than the versions children now hear. Mutilation, starvation, and violent punishment appear routinely in the earliest printed texts, and tracing what happened to that material across two centuries of editing reveals how a culture decides what children may be told. The collectors themselves began the process. Successive editions of the most famous German collection were revised repeatedly by their compilers, who softened sexual material while frequently intensifying violence directed at villains, since punishment was regarded as morally instructive in a way that other content was not. The manuscript versions differ substantially from the published ones, and the differences are systematic rather than casual. Later editing went further. Twentieth century versions for children removed the punishments as well, replaced deaths with escapes, and converted cruel mothers into stepmothers, a change that had already begun with the original compilers. Each revision reflects a judgment about what a child can bear and what an adult wishes to appear to endorse, so the sequence of texts is a record of changing attitudes rather than of the tales themselves. Defenders of the harsher versions argue that the violence performs a function. Such stories present danger, abandonment, and injustice in a form that a child can handle because it is clearly not the world, and removing that content leaves stories that reassure without preparing. This position has been argued by psychologists and by writers who work in the tradition. What the editing history demonstrates is that these narratives were never fixed. They circulated orally in versions adapted to each audience, the collectors created a text by choosing among them, and every subsequent version continued a process that the printing merely interrupted. There is no original from which the later ones departed.

subject: 판소리와 서사 음악의 구조
title: How a sung story is built
content: A full performance in the Korean sung storytelling tradition lasts several hours and is delivered by one singer with one drummer. Its construction is highly organised beneath what sounds to a newcomer like continuous singing, and understanding the structure explains how a single performer sustains a narrative of that length. The performance alternates between two modes. Passages of sung delivery carry the emotional weight, and between them the performer speaks in a heightened narrative voice, advancing the plot, describing the setting, and addressing the audience. The alternation is functional as well as expressive, since the spoken passages let the voice recover from singing that would otherwise be unsustainable, and they move the story quickly through material that does not merit music. Rhythmic cycles organise the sung sections. A limited number of patterns exist, each with a characteristic tempo and character, and the choice among them signals what kind of moment is arriving before any words are heard. A slow expansive cycle marks lament, and a rapid driving one marks urgency or comic bustle, so an audience familiar with the tradition anticipates the emotional direction from the drum alone. Melodic modes work similarly, each associated with a region and a mood. The drummer is a participant rather than an accompanist. Beyond keeping the cycle, they place calls of encouragement at structural points, and an experienced drummer shapes the performance by where those calls fall. Singers describe the relationship as the principal support of a long performance. What holds the whole together is that every element carries information. Tempo, mode, mode of delivery, and drum pattern all tell the listener where they are in the story, which is how an audience follows a narrative of several hours delivered by one voice without any scenery or costume to assist them.

subject: 뜻과 가리킴의 관계
title: How words fasten onto things
content: A name picks out a particular thing, and a general term picks out a kind. How this fastening works is among the central questions in the philosophy of language, and the answers proposed have consequences well beyond linguistics. One traditional account holds that a name works through a description. To use a name is to intend whatever satisfies some associated description, so the name reaches its object by way of what the speaker believes about it. This explains how names can be informative, since discovering that two names pick out one thing tells you something. It faces a serious difficulty. Speakers frequently hold false beliefs about the bearers of names they use competently, and if the description determined the reference, they would be talking about somebody else or about nobody. Yet they plainly succeed in referring, which suggests the mechanism lies elsewhere. A second account locates the fastening in a causal chain. A name is attached to something at some initial point, and it passes from speaker to speaker with the intention of using it as those before did, so a person can refer to somebody they know almost nothing about because they inherited the term from a chain that reaches back to the original attachment. The account extends to natural kinds. A term for a substance picks out whatever shares the underlying nature of the samples originally named, so speakers who could not distinguish that substance from a lookalike were nonetheless referring to it. This yields the conclusion that certain truths about what things are turn out to be necessary while being discoverable only by investigation, which reversed a long standing assumption that necessity and knowledge independent of experience travel together.
